notes.meaning: Joseph receives word that his elderly father is failing in health. He quickly brings his two teenage sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, to Jacob's bedside. Joseph wants them to receive their grandfather's blessing before he dies, valuing God's family far more than royal status in Egypt.

When Jacob hears that his son has arrived, he gathers his remaining strength and sits up in bed. Calling him 'Israel' shows that he is preparing to act with spiritual authority as God's chosen patriarch. He puts his weakness aside so he can pass on God's covenant promises.

Jacob recalls how God Almighty appeared to him years earlier at Luz, also called Bethel, in the land of Canaan. God promised to make him fruitful, multiply his descendants into many nations, and give them that land forever. Before speaking about his grandsons, Jacob anchors everything in God's faithful promises.

Jacob formally adopts Joseph's two sons as his own, giving them the same standing as his eldest sons, Reuben and Simeon. This act gives Joseph the double portion of inheritance that usually belonged to the firstborn. Even though the boys grew up in Egypt, they are brought fully into the family of faith.

Any other children born to Joseph after this will remain his own and will not head their own tribes. Instead, their descendants will share in the land assigned to Ephraim and Manasseh. This decision ensures that Joseph's family receives exactly two tribal portions in Israel.

Jacob pauses to remember his beloved wife Rachel, Joseph's mother, who died on the road near Bethlehem. Rachel died before seeing her son's great honor, so Jacob honors her now by adopting her grandsons as full tribal heads. Remembering her loss also reminds Joseph of the family's true home in Canaan.

Jacob notices the two young men standing near Joseph and asks who they are. Because his eyesight has faded, he cannot clearly make out their faces. This question also marks the formal opening of the blessing ceremony.

Joseph answers with humility, telling his father that these boys are gifts from God. Jacob asks Joseph to bring them close so he can speak God's blessing over them. A dying patriarch's blessing was taken seriously as a solemn and binding word from God.

Jacob's eyes are dim with old age, just as his father Isaac's eyes had been decades earlier. When Joseph brings the young men near, Jacob warmly hugs and kisses them. He shows deep grandfatherly affection before performing his official duty.

Jacob marvels at God's overwhelming goodness. For many painful years, he thought Joseph was dead and that he would never see him again. Now God has blessed him far beyond his hopes by letting him see his grandchildren as well.

Joseph moves his sons back from his father's knees so they can be positioned to receive the blessing. He then bows with his face to the ground. Even as the ruler of Egypt, Joseph shows deep respect to his father and God's chosen prophet.

Joseph places the older son Manasseh toward Jacob's right hand and the younger Ephraim toward his left hand. The right hand was the traditional symbol of greater power and honor. Instead of following the expected pattern, Jacob intentionally crosses his arms to put his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh.

Jacob blesses Joseph through his sons by calling on God under three names: the God his fathers walked before, the God who shepherded him all his life, and the Angel who redeemed him from all harm. Commentators see this redeeming Angel not as a created being, but as the Lord Himself acting as Jacob's protector. Jacob prays that these young men will carry on the family name and multiply into a great multitude.

Joseph is displeased when he sees his father's right hand resting on the younger brother's head. Thinking his father made a mistake because of his failing eyesight, Joseph tries to lift and move Jacob's hand over to the firstborn. He wants natural custom and birth order to be kept.

Jacob refuses to move his hands, assuring his son that he knows what he is doing under God's guidance. While Manasseh will indeed grow into a great and numerous tribe, younger Ephraim will become even greater. This prophecy was fulfilled centuries later when Ephraim became the leading tribe of the northern kingdom.

differ.view: God choosing the younger brother illustrates unconditional election, meaning God chooses people according to His own free will and grace rather than human status or birth order.

notes.meaning: Jacob finishes his blessing by stating that his words will become a standard prayer of well-wishing across future generations of Israel. Parents would bless their sons by praying that God would make them fruitful and honored like Ephraim and Manasseh. By placing Ephraim's name first, Jacob cements the younger brother's special place.

Jacob speaks calmly of his approaching death, reassuring Joseph that God's presence will remain with the family. He promises that God will eventually lead their descendants out of Egypt and back to the land of their fathers. This gave the family hope to look beyond their current comforts in Egypt.

Jacob awards Joseph a special ridge of land above what his brothers will receive, connected to the area of Shechem. Commentators explain the mention of sword and bow either as a prophetic picture of his descendants' future conquest of Canaan, or as a recovery of land Jacob had previously bought. Joseph's bones were later buried in this very ground.
